docs.title: Configure Passes and Inputs
docs.text: The config panel is where you set up shader passes and choose their inputs. Everything is stored in a .sha.json file that the visual editor writes for you.

docs.title: Opening the Config Panel
docs.text: Click the Config button in the toolbar.

docs.title: Pass Cards
docs.text:
The cards at the top show the current shader's passes and their types. Select a card to edit its settings. Click + New to add a pass. Remove a pass with the × on its card (Image cannot be removed).

Click a render pass's eye button to preview its output. The Viewing badge identifies the displayed pass, independently of the selected settings card. Click Image's eye to return to the final output. Compute cards are labeled Compute pass and their settings explain that direct preview is unavailable; Common, Script, and Storage also have no eye button.

While the debugger renders a selected code line, Viewing · L24 follows that line's pass and the label above the canvas also shows the line number. Pass eye buttons are disabled while line rendering controls the output. Turn off line rendering to return to your chosen pass preview.

Right-click a card's name to open a context menu:

  • Open — opens the pass's file in the editor without changing the lock setting
  • Preview this pass — displays a render pass with its configured inputs and Common code; choose this on Image to return to the final output
  • Preview file standalone — makes a buffer's source file the active shader, using its own matching config if present
  • Rename — inline rename for buffer passes (Image, Common, and Script cannot be renamed)
Card Description Image Always present. The final rendered output from the main shader file. Supports mainImage or a selected native WGSL/Slang fragment. No file chooser. Named buffer pass An intermediate fragment render pass backed by a .glsl, .slang, or .wgsl file. Names and pass counts are unrestricted. Compute pass A Slang or WGSL compute pass declared with "type": "compute" and backed by a .slang or .wgsl file. Common Shared functions, constants, and types used by other passes. Script A TypeScript or JavaScript file that drives custom uniform values per frame.

Note

Double-click a pass card's name to open that pass's file. Files linked to the current shader keep its preview visible without locking it. Selecting settings never changes the viewed pass. See Locking and buffer previews.

docs.title: The Image Pass
docs.text:
For WGSL and Slang render passes, Render output shows the active Function. A single selected function appears as text; when more functions are available, use the picker to choose which one renders. A missing configured function stays visible with (missing) so you can correct it.

Choose + Add… to insert either a Native fragment function or Built-in mainImage into the pass's shader file. The built-in action is disabled when mainImage is already present. Adding inserts code; picking a function selects existing code. Changes are saved with the shader configuration.

The Image card has no file path — it always corresponds to your main shader file. You can set a default resolution here:

Setting Options Description Scale 0.25×, 0.5×, 1×, 2×, 4× Relative to the panel size Aspect ratio 16:9, 4:3, 1:1, Fill, Screen Constrains the canvas shape. Screen uses your screen's aspect ratio. Custom dimensions e.g. 1920 × 1080 Base width and height in pixels

The Image pass can also have input channels. GLSL and Slang access them by the configured name, such as iChannel0 or iChannel1; Slang also supports direct channel methods such as iChannel0.Sample(uv). WGSL uses its existing separate texture/sampler handles and free functions such as iChannel0Sample(uv). The .sha.json field remains inputs. See Channels for how to bind textures, video, audio, and more.

See Resolution for how these settings interact with the toolbar.

  • scale and width / height are composable. For example, width: 320, height: 180, scale: 2 renders as 640 × 360.

docs.title: Buffer Passes
docs.text:
Each buffer pass uses a .glsl, .slang, or .wgsl file to produce an image that other passes can sample. Buffer pass names are ordinary identifiers such as Flow, BloomHorizontal, or BufferA; there is no BufferA–BufferD name set or four-pass limit. Every pass can configure its own channels: GLSL uses iChannelN and iChN, Slang uses direct globals such as iChannelN, and WGSL uses free functions such as iChannelNSample(uv). See Channels for how to bind textures, video, audio, and more.

Choose + New → Cubemap to create a cubemap buffer. Its Output section sets the square face size (512 pixels by default). To use the result, add a Buffer channel to a later pass and select the cubemap pass in Misc. Sample it with a three-component direction vector rather than a two-component UV coordinate. See Cubemap Buffers for a complete walkthrough.

The Shader file picker shows the pass's file. Click it to choose from the files already used by the config, or use Browse workspace…, Create file…, or Enter a path… to type one. Open editor opens the pass's file. Several passes can use the same source file, each selecting a different function. Standalone’s Browse action selects files from its virtual workspace.

Three path forms are supported:

Form Example Resolves relative to Relative passes/flow.slang The main shader file Absolute /Users/me/project/flow.glsl Filesystem root Workspace-root @/src/flow.glsl VS Code workspace root (/ of the virtual workspace in the standalone browser host)

Create file… generates a source template using the shader mode preference. For WGSL/Slang, Render output → Function shows the selected fragment function; use the picker when multiple functions are available. + Add… inserts a native fragment function or built-in mainImage into that file. A native fragment can run without mainImage, and native templates use the generated vertex stage until you request a custom one. GLSL has no fragment function selector or Built-in/Native chooser because it uses the fixed mainImage hook.

The pass sections are arranged as Fragment source/functions, Channels, Geometry, Rendering, Resolution, Output, and Vertex shader. Image omits the file chooser. Output selects 2D or Cubemap, its cubemap face size, the buffer format, and read-only inferred output slots and names.

Resolution (optional) — by default a buffer inherits the Image pass resolution exactly. You can override this in two ways:

Mode Example Description Fixed 512 × 512 Exact pixel dimensions, independent of the canvas Scale 0.5× Multiplier on the Image resolution — tracks canvas changes

docs.title: Native Entry Points and Shared Files
docs.text:
Slang and WGSL both run on WebGPU and support this workflow.

An entry point is the function a shader pass runs. WGSL marks these functions with @vertex, @fragment, or @compute; Slang uses [shader("vertex")], [shader("fragment")], or [shader("compute")].

You can keep these functions in one shader file and choose a different function for each pass. In Config, select the function under Fragment shader, Vertex shader, or the compute pass's function list. Add each pass you need with + New; writing another function does not create a pass.

You can also mix a native stage with a Built-in stage. With no custom vertex selection, Shader Studio uses its built-in vertex shader and any configured mainVertex hook. With no native fragment selection, it uses mainImage.

Native fragments receive WebGPU coordinates with a top-left origin; mainImage receives bottom-left coordinates. Native stages still receive Shader Studio's built-in globals, configured channel helpers, and storage declarations. Group 0 bindings are reserved for these generated resources; do not redeclare their bindings. See Vertex Shaders for compatible mesh inputs and transforms.

docs.title: Example: Share a WGSL File
docs.text:
Create a file named shared.wgsl in your shader workspace and paste in this example:

@vertex fn fullscreen(@builtin(vertex_index) index: u32) -> @builtin(position) vec4f {
    let p = array(vec2f(-1, -1), vec2f(3, -1), vec2f(-1, 3));
    return vec4f(p[index], 0, 1);
}

@fragment fn image(@builtin(position) pixel: vec4f) -> @location(0) vec4f {
    return vec4f(pixel.xy / iResolution.xy, 0.5, 1);
}

@compute @workgroup_size(1)
fn advance(@builtin(global_invocation_id) id: vec3u) {
    // Update configured storage here.
}

Save the following configuration as shared.sha.json beside it, then open shared.wgsl in the preview. You should see a red/green gradient with a constant blue component. The example compute function does no work until you add your own code.

{
  "version": "1.0",
  "webgpu": { "defaultRenderAuthoring": "native" },
  "passes": {
    "ComputeAdvance": {
      "type": "compute", "path": "shared.wgsl",
      "entryPoints": { "compute": "advance" },
      "dispatch": { "count": 1 }
    },
    "BufferA": {
      "path": "shared.wgsl",
      "entryPoints": { "vertex": "fullscreen", "fragment": "image" }
    },
    "Image": { "entryPoints": { "vertex": "fullscreen", "fragment": "image" } }
  }
}

Image and BufferA both select fullscreen and image from the same file; ComputeAdvance selects advance. Each pass uses its own configured channels, uniforms, and storage, so you can reuse a file with different inputs. Shared helpers can also live in a Common pass.

docs.title: Cubemap Buffers
docs.text:
A cubemap stores the view in six directions as six square faces. Use a cubemap buffer to generate an environment or reflection texture that other passes can sample. Its face size is independent of the preview canvas size.

GLSL fragment shaders and Slang fragment or compute shaders can generate cubemaps. WGSL cubemap generation is not supported yet.

docs.title: Create and Preview a Cubemap
docs.text:
1. Open a GLSL or Slang shader and choose Config → + New → Cubemap.
  2. In the new pass, click the Shader file picker and choose Create file… to create a starter shader, or choose an existing file containing mainCubemap.
  3. In Output, set Face size (512 pixels by default).
  4. In Preview, choose Face, Cross layout, or Environment to inspect the result. The starter colors each direction differently.
  5. Choose Image output to return to your final shader image.

Changing the preview view does not change the saved shader configuration. Slang cubemap passes also offer Cubemap execution to choose Fragment or Compute.

docs.title: Write the Cubemap Shader
docs.text:
A fragment pass calls mainCubemap once per pixel of every face. fragCoord is the face pixel coordinate, rayOri is zero, and rayDir is the normalized sampling direction:

void mainCubemap(out vec4 color, in vec2 fragCoord,
                 in vec3 rayOri, in vec3 rayDir) {
    color = vec4(rayDir * 0.5 + 0.5, 1.0);
}

float4 mainCubemap(float2 fragCoord, float3 rayOri, float3 rayDir) {
    return float4(rayDir * 0.5 + 0.5, 1.0);
}

docs.title: Sample the Cubemap in Another Pass
docs.text:
In the receiving pass, add a channel such as iChannel0, open Misc, and select the cubemap pass. In GLSL, sample it with texture(iChannel0, direction); in Slang, use iChannel0.Sample(direction).

For example, this GLSL Image shader views the cubemap along the positive Z direction. Place it in your main shader file after connecting iChannel0:

void mainImage(out vec4 fragColor, in vec2 fragCoord) {
    vec2 uv = fragCoord / iResolution.xy * 2.0 - 1.0;
    vec3 direction = normalize(vec3(uv, 1.0));
    fragColor = texture(iChannel0, direction);
}

If you prefer to edit the configuration directly, save the cubemap shader as environment.glsl beside the main shader and use this .sha.json configuration:

{
  "version": "1.0",
  "passes": {
    "Cubemap": {
      "path": "environment.glsl",
      "outputKind": "cubemap",
      "faceSize": 512
    },
    "Image": {
      "inputs": { "iChannel0": { "type": "buffer", "source": "Cubemap" } }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Slang Compute Cubemaps
docs.text: For a Slang compute cubemap, use cubemapDirection(pixel.xy, face) to get the direction for a face pixel and writeOutput(pixel.xy, face, color) to write its color. Face indices 0–5 are +X, −X, +Y, −Y, +Z, and −Z. The default Output texels dispatch covers all six faces; the Z coordinate identifies the face. cubemapDirection samples the center of the pixel.

docs.title: Limits and Feedback
docs.text:
Faces default to 512 pixels and are limited by the device's texture limits. Cubemap passes use fullscreen fragment rendering or Slang compute; custom vertex stages, mesh geometry, multiple outputs, 2D resolution settings, and per-layer channel selection are unavailable. Nearest and linear filtering use the base level; generated mipmaps are not provided.

For feedback effects, connect the cubemap pass to one of its own channels: it reads its previous frame, starting from a cleared image. Later passes read all six faces from the current frame. Changing Face size or pressing Reset clears the feedback history. Resizing the preview canvas keeps the configured face size.

docs.title: Per-Pass Geometry
docs.text:
Each buffer and Image pass can render with 2D or 3D geometry. Open the Geometry dropdown in the pass config to choose:

Geometry Description Fullscreen One triangle covering the screen (default). Standard 2D shader rendering. Vertices Any number of vertices placed by the vertex shader, joined as triangles, lines, or points, in world space (seen by the orbit camera) or clip space (fixed on screen). Set Vertices, Topology and Space below the dropdown. Plane A flat 3D plane. Cube A unit cube centred at the origin. Sphere A UV-mapped sphere. Model A custom GLB mesh.

The Vertex shader section appears last: after Resolution for Image and after Output for render buffers. Choose Built-in, Same file, or Separate file. Separate file shows its path and Change… chooser; Same file hides the duplicate path. Vertex function rows come from the selected vertex source. Add function… inserts into that source. GLSL shows only Add when mainVertex is missing, without a function selector or mode chooser. See Vertex Shaders for details on writing vertex shaders and the mainVertex API, and Vertices geometry for vertexCount, topology and space.

The Rendering section after Geometry sets the pass's Blend mode, and for every geometry but fullscreen its Depth test, Depth write, Compare and Cull. See Render settings.

docs.title: GPU Storage
docs.text: Each storage buffer has its own card, labeled Storage buffer with its element count. Select it to open Settings / Inspect directly. Choose + New → Storage buffer to add one. Apply pending settings from the header or below the form. See GPU Storage for layouts, binary initial data, resets and read-only inspection.

docs.title: Compute Passes
docs.text: Use + New → Compute to add a compute pass, then use the Shader file picker to select, reuse, or create its .slang or .wgsl source. Choose a compute function row or use Add function…. Compute has Channels, Dispatch, Execution, and Output settings, with no Built-in mode, vertex stage, or geometry section. See Compute Passes for shader examples, storage buffers, and dispatch settings.

docs.title: The Script Pass
docs.text: The Script pass drives custom uniform values per frame from a TypeScript or JavaScript file. Use it to animate parameters or bring external data into your shader.

docs.title: Exporting Uniforms
docs.text:
Your script must export a uniforms(ctx) function that returns an object:

// shader.uniforms.ts
export function uniforms(ctx: {
  iTime: number;
  iFrame: number;
  iTimeDelta: number;
  iFrameRate: number;
  iResolution: [number, number, number];
  iMouse: [number, number, number, number];
  iDate: [number, number, number, number];
  iSampleRate: number;
  iChannelTime: [number, number, number, number];
}) {
  return {
    uSpeed:   ctx.iTime * 0.5,
    uColor:   [Math.sin(ctx.iTime), 0.5, 1.0] as [number, number, number],
    uEnabled: true,
  };
}

docs.title: Type Inference
docs.text:
Types are inferred from the return value on the first call. Use the returned names directly in your shader without declaring them.

Return type GLSL uniform number uniform float uSpeed; [n, n] uniform vec2 uOffset; [n, n, n] uniform vec3 uColor; [n, n, n, n] uniform vec4 uRect; boolean uniform bool uEnabled;

WGSL and Slang shaders receive the same values as globals with the script's field names — no declaration needed. WGSL uses f32, vec2<f32>, vec3<f32>, vec4<f32>, and bool; Slang uses the corresponding float, floatN, and bool types.

docs.title: Polling Rate
docs.text:
The Max Polling Rate slider (1–120 fps) controls how often the script runs. The config panel shows the actual vs. target polling rate for each uniform.

For slowly-changing values, 1–10 fps is usually enough. High rates consume more CPU.

docs.title: Using Node.js APIs
docs.text:
Scripts run in Node.js and can require() any module. Modules resolve from the script file's own directory.

import * as fs from 'fs';

export function uniforms(ctx) {
  const data = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('./params.json', 'utf8'));
  return { uValue: data.value };
}

Because the script runs in Node.js, you can pull in values from anywhere — game controllers, serial ports, external hardware, WebSockets, OS sensors, or any npm package. For example, you could read a gamepad with a library like node-hid, stream data from a microcontroller over serial, or poll an external API for live data.

Warning

Do not name script uniforms the same as built-ins (iTime, iResolution, iChannel0, etc.). The script will fail to load with an error listing the collision.

docs.title: The Common Pass
docs.text:
Use the Common pass for shared utility functions, constants, and types. Select a .glsl, .slang, or .wgsl file written in the same language as your other passes.

GLSLSlang 
// shader.common.glsl — available in Image, BufferA, etc.
#define PI 3.14159265359

float hash(vec2 p) {
    return fract(sin(dot(p, vec2(127.1, 311.7))) * 43758.5453);
}

float noise(vec2 p) {
    vec2 i = floor(p);
    vec2 f = fract(p);
    float a = hash(i);
    float b = hash(i + vec2(1.0, 0.0));
    float c = hash(i + vec2(0.0, 1.0));
    float d = hash(i + vec2(1.0, 1.0));
    vec2 u = f * f * (3.0 - 2.0 * f);
    return mix(a, b, u.x) + (c - a) * u.y * (1.0 - u.x) + (d - b) * u.x * u.y;
}

// shader.common.slang — available in Image, BufferA, etc.
#define PI 3.14159265359

float hash(float2 p) {
    return fract(sin(dot(p, float2(127.1, 311.7))) * 43758.5453);
}

float noise(float2 p) {
    float2 i = floor(p);
    float2 f = fract(p);
    float a = hash(i);
    float b = hash(i + float2(1.0, 0.0));
    float c = hash(i + float2(0.0, 1.0));
    float d = hash(i + float2(1.0, 1.0));
    float2 u = f * f * (3.0 - 2.0 * f);
    return lerp(a, b, u.x) + (c - a) * u.y * (1.0 - u.x) + (d - b) * u.x * u.y;
}

You can then use hash, noise, or PI in any Image or named buffer pass.

Note

Common provides shared code; it does not produce an image of its own.

docs.title: Other: Editing the Config File Directly
docs.text:
The config is stored as JSON in a .sha.json file with the same base name as the shader (myshader.glsl, myshader.slang, or myshader.wgsl → myshader.sha.json), in the same directory. You can edit it directly in VS Code, and the Config panel stays in sync with the file.

See Config File Format for the full schema reference.

docs.title: Editor Overlay
docs.text:
The editor overlay lets you write shader code directly on top of the preview canvas. You see the shader output behind the code as you type, so you don't have to switch back and forth between the editor and the preview.

The overlay includes editor features designed to feel similar to the VS Code editor.

docs.title: Opening
docs.text:
• Click the Editor icon in the toolbar
  • Or run Shader Studio: Toggle Editor Overlay from the command palette

docs.title: Working with Multiple Passes
docs.text:
When your shader has multiple passes — Image, BufferA, BufferB, Common, and so on — each appears as a tab along the top of the overlay. Click a tab to switch to that pass. Changes you make are saved back to the file automatically.

Double-click a buffer tab in the config panel to open that pass. See Locking to keep the preview on your main shader while editing other files.

docs.title: Vim Mode
docs.text:
If you prefer Vim keybindings, open the options menu while the overlay is enabled and select Vim Mode.

Vim mode supports the standard editing motions provided by the embedded editor, including / search:

Key Action / Search forward in the overlay

docs.title: GLSL Support
docs.text:
GLSL shaders (.glsl) use WebGL2. GLSL is the original Shader Studio language: fragment shaders use mainImage, optional vertex shaders use the vertex hook (see Vertex Shaders), and buffer passes compose multipass projects (see Configure Buffers And Inputs).

Named channel metadata and sampling examples are in Channels.

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
• Editing: completion, hover, go to definition, references, highlights, and rename. Diagnostics report unresolved symbols and unused locals. See Language Servers for editor instructions and rename scope.
  • Rendering: single pass, multipass buffers, Common, vertex shaders, textures, cubemaps, audio/video inputs, keyboard input, model geometry and script custom uniforms. Compute passes and storage buffers are not available for GLSL.
  • Debugging: inline rendering and fragment-stage variable capture work, including inside Common helpers.
  • Hosts: VS Code extension and standalone browser.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• No workspace symbol search (all languages).
  • No vertex-stage debugging (all languages).

Back to the full matrix: Language Support.

docs.title: Language Servers
docs.text:
Shader Studio includes editor support for GLSL, Slang, and WGSL. No additional shader extension is needed.

All three services are enabled by default. Open a shader file in VS Code and use the normal editor features such as completion (Ctrl+Space), hover, and Go to Definition.

docs.title: Supported Editor Features
docs.text:
Feature GLSL Slang WGSL Completion Yes Yes Yes Hover documentation Yes Yes Yes Signature help Yes Yes Yes Go to Definition Yes Yes Yes Document symbols / Outline Yes Yes Yes Find references / highlight Yes Yes Yes Rename Yes Yes, with limits below Yes Error checking Syntax checks Syntax and type checks Basic checks as you type; full checks when compiling Color decorators and picker vec3 and vec4 literals float3 and float4 literals vec3f/vec4f and vec3<f32>/vec4<f32> literals

Completion and hover include:

  • Language intrinsics such as GLSL texture, Slang fmod, and WGSL dot
  • Shader Studio uniforms such as iResolution, iTime, and channel inputs
  • Shader Studio channel objects such as Slang iChannel0, plus WGSL free-function accessors such as iChannel0Sample(uv)
  • Functions, structures, and variables declared in the current shader
  • Functions and types provided by configured Common and dependency files
  • Custom uniforms from the active Script and resources from the Shader Studio configuration
  • Entry points and built-ins for fragment, vertex, and compute shaders

Hover shows local and parameter types, struct fields, and vector components. Slang and WGSL also describe channel access and configured storage. Signature help follows nested calls; Slang supports generic calls such as bit_cast<uint>(.

docs.title: WGSL Diagnostics
docs.text:
WGSL has no user-defined generics, function overloads, or import/include mechanism; put shared code in Common.

As you type, the editor reports syntax errors, undefined names, reserved words, and uses of built-ins or discard in an incompatible shader stage. It reports the first syntax error; fix that error to see name and stage diagnostics. To check expression types, function arguments, and return values, compile your shader. Errors point to the relevant shader, Common, or vertex file where possible.

When editing Common, syntax errors appear as you type. Compile a pass that uses Common to check its helpers fully. If a helper uses an operation unavailable in that pass, such as dpdx in compute code, the error identifies the helper and line.

Signature help shows named parameters and documentation for authored, Common, channel, and built-in functions. Add leading // comments to document your own functions. Signature help also works inside nested calls and template arguments.

Vector component completion includes all valid one-to-four-component read selections, including reordered and repeated forms such as yx, xxxx, and bgra.

docs.title: References and Rename
docs.text:
Use Find All References to find uses of an authored symbol. Results can include configured Common and dependency files; document highlights mark occurrences in the current editor. Search is limited to the shader's known sources, not every file in the workspace. Formatting and workspace symbol search are unavailable.

Use Rename Symbol (F2) to rename a function, parameter, variable, or struct field. Both VS Code and the standalone editor can update affected shader and Common files. All target files must be available and writable for the edits to be applied. This is separate from renaming a shader file in the explorer.

Slang rename handles local names and overloaded functions, and checks that the change does not introduce errors. It can also update generic helpers, methods, and imports. If a symbol cannot be identified safely or the change would fail validation, the rename is declined.

docs.title: Color Picker
docs.text:
With shader-studio.editor.colorDecorators enabled, literal constructors show a small VS Code color swatch:

vec4 accent = vec4(1.0, 0.5, 0.0, 1.0);

float4 accent = float4(1.0, 0.5, 0.0, 1.0);

var accent = vec4f(1.0, 0.5, 0.0, 1.0);
var glow = vec3<f32>(0.0, 0.5, 1.0);

Picking a color rewrites only the literal arguments, so a vec3<f32> stays a vec3<f32> with three components.

docs.title: Spell Checking
docs.text: If you use the optional Code Spell Checker (streetsidesoftware.code-spell-checker) extension, Shader Studio registers a bundled dictionary containing common GLSL, Slang, WebGPU, and Shader Studio terms.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Setting Default Description shader-studio.languageServers.glsl.enabled true Enable or disable GLSL language features. shader-studio.languageServers.slang.enabled true Enable or disable Slang language features. shader-studio.languageServers.wgsl.enabled true Enable or disable WGSL language features. shader-studio.editor.colorDecorators true Show editable swatches for literal shader colors.

docs.title: Language Support
docs.text: Shader Studio supports GLSL on WebGL2 and Slang and WGSL on WebGPU. This page compares the editor, rendering, and debugging features that are available in each language.

docs.text:
Feature GLSL Slang WGSL Completion, hover, and definition Yes Yes Yes References / highlights Yes Yes Yes Rename Yes Yes, with limits Yes Workspace symbol search No No No Error checking Syntax checks Syntax and type checks Basic checks as you type; full checks when compiling Signature help Yes Yes Yes Color swatches vec3 / vec4 float3 / float4 vec3f / vec4f and vec3<f32> / vec4<f32>

See Language Servers for editor instructions and rename scope.

docs.text:
Feature GLSL Slang WGSL Single pass / multipass / Common Yes Yes Yes Vertex shaders Yes Yes Yes Compute No Yes Yes Storage buffers No Yes Yes Texture / cubemap / audio / video / keyboard inputs Yes Yes Yes Named channel metadata Yes Yes Yes; texture and sampler handles are separate Model geometry Yes Yes Yes Custom uniforms from script Yes Yes Yes

See Channels for the public channel API and compatibility details.

docs.text:
Feature GLSL Slang WGSL Inline rendering Yes Yes Yes Variable capture (fragment) Yes Yes Yes 2x2 matrix capture mat2 float2x2 mat2x2f, mat2x2<f32> Vertex-stage debugging No No No Compute-pass debugging No One invocation at a time One invocation at a time Inspect values in Common helpers Yes Yes Yes Inspect values read from storage No Yes Yes

The languages share the same debugger controls, but they do not have identical syntax or capture types. See the Variable Inspector for supported values.

docs.title: WGSL Syntax Differences
docs.text:
Slang and WGSL share the WebGPU rendering workflows above, with differences in shader syntax:

  • Channel metadata uses dot access; native handles stay separate. Use albedo.size, .time, and .loaded, then sample with sample2D(albedoTexture, albedoSampler, uv). Slang uses the same function name with albedo.texture and albedo.sampler. WGSL cannot put handles in structs or expose Slang's optional methods. Legacy per-channel functions remain available; see Channels.
  • The vertex hook takes pointers. WGSL has no inout parameters, so mainVertex receives ptr<function, …> pointers and you modify the pointed-to values: 
    fn mainVertex(vertexIndex: u32, position: ptr<function, vec3<f32>>, normal: ptr<function, vec3<f32>>, uv: ptr<function, vec2<f32>>) {
    (*position).y += 0.1 * sin(iTime);
}
    See Vertex Shaders.
  • Assign single components, not swizzles. Assigning a swizzle (position.xy = ...) requires support for the optional swizzle_assignment language feature. For compatibility across browsers and VS Code, write the components separately or replace the whole vector: 
    let nudged = (*position).xy + offset;
(*position).x = nudged.x;
(*position).y = nudged.y;

body.velocity = vec4f(body.velocity.xyz + force, body.velocity.w);
  • No imports. Put shared functions and types in the Common pass, as with GLSL.
  • No preprocessor. There is no #define, #if, or macro expansion. Use const / override declarations and plain WGSL control flow instead. Snippets that relied on the GLSL preprocessor will not translate line-for-line.
  • enable directives are supported. Use enable, requires, and diagnostic() directives at the top of your shader or Common file. If an enable names an extension the GPU does not support (for example enable f16; on hardware without shader-f16), compilation fails with an error naming the missing requirement.

docs.title: Hosts and Limitations
docs.text:
The VS Code extension and standalone browser support all three languages. Slang and WGSL require WebGPU; GLSL uses WebGL2.

  • Matrix capture supports 2x2 matrices; select individual columns or components for larger matrices. See WGSL capture types.
  • Compute debugging cannot reproduce threads working together in a workgroup. See Slang debugging and WGSL compute limits.
  • Whole arrays, structs, and arbitrary pointers are not capture rows; inspect supported elements or fields instead.
  • Workspace symbol search and vertex-stage debugging are unavailable.

Language details: GLSL · Slang · WGSL syntax.

docs.title: Locking a Shader
docs.text: Opening a buffer, Common file, or vertex file referenced by the current shader keeps that shader's preview visible. This does not lock the preview. Opening an unrelated shader switches the preview. Click the Lock button to keep the current shader visible even when you open unrelated shader files.

docs.title: Why Locking Matters
docs.text:
Multi-buffer shaders have an Image pass and one or more buffer passes (like BufferA, BufferB). You can edit their linked files while watching the final image without enabling Lock.

Locking is useful when editing an unrelated shader: the preview stays on the locked shader instead of following your new file selection.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
1. Open the shader you want to keep visible
  2. Click the Lock button in the toolbar — the icon will show as locked
  3. Open any buffer file to edit it — the preview stays on the locked shader
  4. Click the button again to unlock when you want the preview to follow your file selection again

Hover over the Lock button to see whether the preview follows the active shader file or stays on the current shader, and what clicking the button will do.

Shader Explorer can also keep each preview's source files open. That setting manages editor tabs and asks before closing unsaved changes. It follows the shader actually displayed in each preview, so a locked preview retains its files.

docs.title: Double-Clicking Pass Cards
docs.text:
Double-click a pass card's name in the config panel to open that pass's file. Opening a pass preserves the current shader context and does not change the lock setting.

  • If you have locked the shader, the preview stays on it while you edit the buffer
  • If the editor overlay is open, it switches to the double-clicked pass's file
  • If the overlay is closed, the pass's file opens in the VS Code editor

docs.title: Preview a Buffer
docs.text:
Click a render pass card's eye button to see its output with the current shader's inputs and Common code. The Viewing badge marks the previewed pass; selecting a different settings card does not change the output. Click Image's eye to return to the final output. The same action is available as Preview this pass in the card's right-click menu.

Choose Preview file standalone in a buffer card's right-click menu to make its source file the active shader. This uses that file's own matching .sha.json, if present, rather than the parent's inputs. A buffer that requires the parent's Common code or inputs may fail to compile standalone. This explicit choice preserves the lock setting; a manual lock moves to the chosen file.

Only the current shader's known file links determine whether opening a file keeps its parent preview. Shader Studio does not search other configs to find an owner. Opening an unlinked buffer file therefore treats it as a standalone shader, even if another shader elsewhere references it.
