docs.title: Connect an AI Assistant
docs.text:
Connect a compatible AI assistant to Shader Studio so it can help edit your shaders, explain errors, inspect values, and see images from your running preview. The connection uses Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard supported by many AI tools.

This feature requires the VS Code extension, a trusted workspace, and an AI tool with a Streamable HTTP MCP client running on the same computer. It works with previews in VS Code and previews opened from VS Code in your browser. The standalone browser app does not provide this connection.

docs.title: Enable the Connection
docs.text:
1. Run Shader Studio: Connect AI Assistant from the Command Palette.
  2. Turn on Enable AI connection. The connection is off by default and requires a trusted workspace.
  3. When the server is ready, the screen shows your Server URL and Token with copy buttons. Use Show token if you need to read it.
  4. Add the connection to your assistant, or use Copy setup prompt to ask a local assistant to help configure it.
  5. Open a Shader Studio preview. The connection screen changes from Waiting for an assistant to Assistant connected after an assistant completes its MCP handshake.

The setup prompt includes your private token and instructions to configure the connection, check it with a tool call, and read Shader Studio's bundled documentation. Paste it only into the local assistant you want to connect. An assistant that cannot change its own MCP settings will need you to complete its setup steps; it may also need a restart.

Once enabled, the connection starts automatically when you launch VS Code. Turn off Enable AI connection to disconnect assistants and stop access. You do not need to run a separate helper program.

docs.title: Set Up Any Compatible Assistant
docs.text:
In your assistant's MCP settings, add a server with these values:

Setting Value Name shader-studio Connection type Streamable HTTP Server URL Copy Server URL from the connection screen (default: http://127.0.0.1:51474/mcp) Bearer token Copy Token from the connection screen

If the assistant asks for HTTP headers instead of a Bearer token, add an Authorization header with the value Bearer YOUR_PRIVATE_TOKEN, replacing YOUR_PRIVATE_TOKEN with the copied token. Keep the token in private local client settings, outside shared shader projects.

Restart or reload the assistant if it needs this to load new MCP servers. Ask it to list Shader Studio previews to confirm it can use the tools.

Assistant connected counts initialized MCP sessions, rather than checking whether an assistant process is running. Unused sessions are cleaned up automatically: idle sessions expire after 30 minutes, and unfinished connections expire after one minute. When capacity is reached, the oldest idle session can be reclaimed sooner. Open streams and requests in progress are kept. If an assistant reports an expired session, reconnect it. The Check server action tests the local endpoint separately and does not count as an assistant connection.

docs.title: Advanced Settings
docs.text:
Expand Advanced settings on the connection screen to:

  • Change port when another VS Code window or application is using the default port. Update your assistant's URL after changing it.
  • Check server to confirm the endpoint accepts the current token and exposes its tools. This does not prove your assistant has been configured.
  • Regenerate token if the token was exposed. Copy the new token into your assistant's private configuration and reconnect.

The token is stored in VS Code Secret Storage. A client running on another computer cannot use this local connection.

docs.title: Ask for Help with a Shader
docs.text:
Try a request like:

Look at my Shader Studio preview and explain how the effect works. Make the colors warmer, check for errors, and show me the updated result. Leave the edits open for me to review.

You can also ask the assistant to:

  • Find and explain a compilation error.
  • Edit a buffer or compute shader and inspect its effect on the final image.
  • Pause the preview and compare values in a Slang or WGSL storage buffer.
  • Adjust playback speed or try a temporary custom-uniform value.
  • Capture a PNG of the current shader output.

If several previews are open, tell the assistant which shader you want to work on. It can list the previews and select the appropriate one. File editing still works when no preview is open; viewing the rendered result requires an open, responsive preview.

docs.title: Review and Save Edits
docs.text:
The assistant can edit your existing shader files and .sha.json configuration in VS Code, or create a new workspace text file with create_file. New files must not already exist. Text changes remain unsaved, and you can review or undo them in the editor. Save the files when you want to keep the changes on disk. The tools do not delete files.

File editing supports local text files up to 1 MB in your workspace or already open in VS Code. Binary assets cannot be edited with these tools. If a file has changed since the assistant read it, it must read the latest version before editing again.

The assistant can wait for compilation and request an updated image after an edit. If compilation fails, the preview may still show the last successful result; ask it to check the errors before evaluating the image. A failed image request does not undo an edit that has already been applied.

Playback and uniform adjustments made through the connection are temporary. A running Script pass may replace a temporary uniform value. To keep a change with the shader, ask the assistant to edit its configuration or script. Seeking to a time does not replay earlier simulation steps; use Reset when you need to restart a simulation.

get_inputs is a live-preview snapshot, not a frozen per-pass GPU capture. It reports built-ins available for the selected preview and identifies values unavailable for that view. When playback is paused, each custom uniform can include its pausedValue; it is null while playback is running. Custom uniform defaults and ranges are reported as unknown when the Script API has not declared them.

docs.title: Tools Available to Your Assistant
docs.text:
You do not need to call these tools yourself. This reference explains what your assistant can do after connecting.

Tool Purpose list_previews Find open VS Code and browser previews list_files Find files in your workspace read_file / update_file Read or edit an existing text file, checking for intervening changes get_shader Read the shader shown in a selected preview get_resources Find the shader's passes, associated files, and storage buffers get_inputs Inspect current live preview inputs and whether a Script pass may overwrite a temporary custom-uniform value get_settings Read the shader configuration and current preview settings update_settings Try temporary playback, frame-rate, or uniform settings get_diagnostics Read current shader errors and warnings start_log_collection / get_logs / stop_log_collection Explicitly collect and read a bounded diagnostic log capture_output Capture a PNG of the rendered result set_playback Pause, resume, seek, or reset the shader read_storage Inspect a range of values in a Slang or WGSL storage buffer read_documentation Read bundled, version-matched MCP, uniforms, pass, channel, compute, storage, and render-output reference topics create_file Create a new workspace text file when it does not already exist select_shader Switch one explicitly selected preview to a shader path inject_input Send canonical pointer and keyboard input events to one explicitly selected preview start_input_recording / stop_input_recording / get_input_recording Capture and inspect a bounded timeline of live input events replay_inputs / get_input_replay / cancel_input_replay Replay a recorded input timeline and inspect or cancel it read_feedback Read a bounded feedback/pass pixel region when the selected backend exposes it start_recording / stop_recording / get_recording Create and monitor a bounded live MP4 or WebM recording; completed artifacts are returned as MCP resources start_frame_capture / get_frame_capture / cancel_frame_capture Capture up to eight PNG frames at requested wall-clock offsets, without creating a video

Capturing an image can advance feedback buffers. For stable comparisons of storage values, pause playback before inspecting them. Storage reads return up to 1,024 elements and 64 KiB at a time; GLSL storage inspection is unavailable.

WebGL read_feedback returns the latest published feedback buffer as up to 4,096 RGBA pixels (64 KiB of float data), using a bottom-left origin. Finite samples are JSON numbers; non-finite samples are the strings NaN, Infinity, or -Infinity. WebGPU uses the separate read_storage tool for numerical storage inspection.

docs.title: Input Automation and Recordings
docs.text:
MCP preview tracking is active only while MCP is enabled in a trusted workspace. Disabling MCP detaches existing previews, cancels pending requests, and clears collected logs. Enabling it again discovers previews that are already open.

Log collection is off by default, even with MCP enabled. Ask the assistant to call start_log_collection before reproducing a problem, then get_logs to inspect it. Collection automatically stops after 60 seconds by default; duration accepts 1–300 seconds. stop_log_collection ends it early. Reads never start or extend collection. One shared collection retains at most 500 messages of up to 4,096 characters each in memory; starting again clears the previous history. Stopped or expired results remain readable until the next start or until MCP is disabled. previewId filters viewer messages while still including extension and Script messages. Shader Studio's ordinary output and Script console behavior remain available independently of MCP collection.

Screenshots, timed frames, videos, and input traces are captured only when explicitly requested. Merely enabling MCP or listing previews does not capture them.

Input injection, replay, feedback reads, and video recording always require an explicit previewId from list_previews. This avoids sending interaction to the wrong preview when several are open. Input events use canonical pointer_move, pointer_down, pointer_up, key_down, key_up, and release_all records (up to 256 events per injection); pointer movement and down events require coordinates, while key events require a key code.

An input recording captures interaction delivered to the selected preview. Replay can reset before it starts, but seeking cannot recreate feedback-buffer history. Use reset and replay from the beginning when comparing a simulation. A preview switch or recompilation is reported in recording metadata.

replay_inputs uses the selected preview’s last input trace. Choose from-current to keep the current simulation state or reset-and-play to reset first. start_recording makes a Live MP4 or WebM artifact for 0.1–60 seconds at 1–60 fps and up to 1920×1080. Set recordInputs to preserve the paired input trace. Its output size does not resize the preview or reset its feedback state. get_recording reports output availability, requested and actual settings, frame timestamps, shader path, compile and render sequences, plus preview-switch and recompile flags. Actual dropped-frame statistics are null when the browser encoder cannot provide them. Read the completed shader-studio://recordings/ID resource (or the resource link returned by the tool) to retrieve the bounded artifact.

Recording storage retains the ten newest completed videos, with a 32 MiB limit per video. Saving another recording deletes older completed videos and abandoned recording .part files older than 24 hours, including leftovers from a previous extension session. Recent partial transfers are preserved for other open VS Code windows. Timed PNG capture jobs stay in preview memory and retain only three completed jobs.

start_frame_capture accepts one to eight sorted, unique requested offsets from 0 to 60 seconds and captures PNGs at up to 1920×1080 (800×450 by default). The job uses real elapsed wall time: each returned frame includes its requested timestamp and its actual elapsed timestamp, which can differ when rendering is late. It never seeks, so feedback advances naturally. Choose reset-and-play only when a fresh simulation is wanted; it performs a real reset and resume before capture. Completed frame images appear in requested-time order in the MCP response; metadata excludes image bytes.

docs.title: Use a Browser Preview
docs.text:
Start Shader Studio's web server from the VS Code status-bar menu, then choose Open in Browser. Your assistant can inspect that preview through the same connection while you continue editing in VS Code.

While MCP is enabled, the web server also accepts connections at http://127.0.0.1:WEB_SERVER_PORT/mcp. Replace WEB_SERVER_PORT with your configured web server port and use the same token. The dedicated MCP address above continues to work too.

See Open in Browser for the preview setup.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem What to do Cannot connect Open Shader Studio: Connect AI Assistant, check that the connection is enabled and ready, and confirm your workspace is trusted and the URL matches your assistant settings. Open VS Code's Output panel and choose Shader Studio for startup errors. Port already in use Choose another Mcp Port for this workspace and update your assistant's URL. Unauthorized / 401 Copy the current Token from Shader Studio: Connect AI Assistant, update your assistant's Bearer token or Authorization header, then restart or reload the client. No preview found Open a Shader Studio panel or a browser preview launched from VS Code. Wrong preview Ask the assistant to list previews and select the shader you mean. File changed Ask the assistant to read the file again before making the edit. Session expired Reconnect after restarting VS Code or changing connection settings. Preview timed out Make the preview visible, check for errors, and try the image request again. Check whether the file edit already succeeded before repeating it.

docs.title: Multiple render targets
docs.text:
A native WGSL or Slang buffer fragment can write several color textures in one draw. Each texture shares the buffer's resolution and floating-point output format. Image remains a single canvas output; GLSL MRT is not supported.

Declare contiguous color locations starting at zero:

struct Outputs {
  @location(0) color: vec4f,
  @location(1) normal: vec4f,
}
@fragment fn shade() -> Outputs {
  return Outputs(vec4f(1, 0, 0, 1), vec4f(0, 0, 1, 1));
}

Slang uses float4 fields with SV_Target0, SV_Target1, and so on. Declaration order does not change attachment indices. A depth result (frag_depth or SV_Depth) is separate from color outputs.

Shader Studio infers the attachment count, slots, and default names from the selected fragment's return declaration. Select the fragment function and connect an output in a downstream input; no outputs list is required:

{
  "version": "1.0",
  "passes": {
    "BufferA": {
      "path": "scene.wgsl",
      "entryPoints": { "fragment": "shade" },
      "outputFormat": "rgba16float"
    },
    "Image": {
      "inputs": {
        "iChannel0": { "type": "buffer", "source": "BufferA", "output": 1 }
      }
    }
  }
}

Omitting an input's output selects attachment zero. Compute outputs continue to use layer; render attachments use output. The consuming channel still needs an explicit choice when you want a nonzero attachment: code discovery cannot decide which texture that channel should sample.

The buffer's Output section shows read-only rows such as Output 0 · color and Output 1 · normal, alongside the shared Output format setting. Add or remove fields in your fragment return type to change the attachments. The UI does not rewrite shader code or add attachments. Older outputs arrays remain optional labels by slot; they do not determine the count or create missing attachments.

Discovery reads the pass source and Common declarations. WGSL supports direct @location(0) returns, return structs, and aliases to those types. Slang supports direct SV_Target returns and structs with SV_TargetN fields. Slots must be unique and contiguous from zero; color values must be four-component float vectors. Missing functions, incomplete return declarations, and invalid slot layouts produce an error instead of inventing outputs. A Built-in mainImage pass has one color output; multiple attachments require a native fragment.

docs.title: Choose an Output in a Channel
docs.text:
1. Configure the consuming channel, such as Image's iChannel0, and open Misc.
  2. Select the source buffer. For multiple attachments, Buffer output lists a separate radio row for each slot and its inferred field name.
  3. Select the desired output. This saves the channel's output number; changing the field name does not change that slot.

Filter and wrap remain channel settings. For a compute source, Misc offers Compute output layer when the source has several layers. If an edited fragment removes the selected attachment, the channel shows that it is unavailable until you choose a valid one.

docs.title: Try Two WGSL Outputs
docs.text:
Paste this into a WGSL buffer source, select @fragment twoOutputs, and leave its vertex source Built-in:

struct BufferOutputs {
    @location(0) colour: vec4f,
    @location(1) inverse: vec4f,
}

@fragment
fn twoOutputs(
    @builtin(position) position: vec4f
) -> BufferOutputs {
    let uv = fract(position.xy / 256.0);

    return BufferOutputs(
        vec4f(uv, 0.0, 1.0),
        vec4f(1.0 - uv, 1.0, 1.0)
    );
}

In Image, bind a channel to that buffer through Misc. Switch between Output 0 · colour and Output 1 · inverse to see two different gradients. The Image shader must sample that channel; for a Built-in WGSL Image hook:

fn mainImage(coord: vec2f) -> vec4f {
    let uv = coord / iResolution.xy;
    return iChannel0Sample(uv);
}

Select mainImage in Image's fragment function rows if it previously used a native fragment. The main Image file and buffer source can be separate files or share one file, with the correct function selected for each pass.

docs.title: Limits and Debugging
docs.text:
The available count depends on the device's attachment count and bytes per sample. rgba16float uses 8 bytes per attachment and rgba32float uses 16. Five rgba16float outputs therefore require at least five attachments and 40 bytes per sample. Shader Studio requests supported limits and reports an error when a configuration exceeds them. All attachments swap together for feedback and share resize/reset behavior.

Native previews and capture retain the authored vertex stage, interpolated inputs, viewer camera, and depth. Variable capture renders to scratch attachments and snapshots storage buffers, so it leaves live output textures and storage unchanged. Select the output in the debug panel to preview or post-process its color. Other fragment output fields remain intact during instrumentation.

Runnable WGSL and Slang examples are in tests/fixtures/shader-corpus/*/native-mrt/.

Shadertoy imports keep their single-output mainImage behavior and existing connections select output zero. Native MRT projects cannot be pasted directly into Shadertoy. Porting them requires splitting outputs into separate passes or packing several values into one texture; splitting can duplicate calculations and lose the benefit of writing several outputs in one draw. Shader Studio does not convert MRT projects automatically.

docs.title: Panel Layout
docs.text:
Shader Studio uses a dockable panel system. Panels (Preview, Debug, Config, Performance) can be rearranged:

  • Drag a tab header to move a panel to a different group
  • Drag to an edge (left, right, top, bottom) of an existing group to split it
  • Drag the sash (the divider between panels) to resize
  • Tab headers auto-hide when only one panel is in a group. To view the tabs again, move your mouse near the top of the panel and they will appear

Choose Menu → Layout → Save current layout to save your changes to the active profile.

docs.title: Layout profiles
docs.text:
Layout profiles let you save and switch between named panel arrangements. Each profile stores:

  • Panel layout (which panels are open, their sizes and positions)
  • Config panel visibility
  • Debug panel visibility and settings
  • Performance panel visibility
  • Theme (in non-VS Code environments)

Open the profile controls from Menu → Layout. The layout submenu shows the active profile, saved profiles, save/restore/reset actions, and Manage profiles.

docs.title: Managing profiles
docs.text:
The Manage Profiles modal lists all saved profiles. The active profile is highlighted.

  • Click a profile name to switch to it immediately
  • Drag the grip handle (left edge of each row) to reorder profiles
  • Rename (pencil icon) — click to edit the name inline; press Enter to confirm or Escape to cancel
  • Save to profile (disk icon, active profile only) — overwrites the profile with the current layout; shows an "Are you sure?" confirmation before saving
  • Delete (trash icon) — removes the profile; disabled when only one profile exists

At the bottom of the modal, enter a name and click Save to create a new profile from the current layout.

docs.title: Saving vs switching
docs.text: Switching profiles loads the saved panel arrangement. Your current layout is not automatically saved when you switch — unsaved changes are discarded. To preserve your current layout, save it first using Menu → Layout → Save current layout or create a new profile.

docs.title: Restoring or resetting layout
docs.text:
Use Menu → Layout → Restore Saved Layout to discard unsaved changes and reload the active profile's saved layout. If the active profile has no saved layout yet, Shader Studio falls back to the default arrangement.

Use Menu → Layout → Reset to Default to rebuild the default panel arrangement directly. This does not overwrite the active profile until you save the current layout.

docs.title: Default profile
docs.text: Every new workspace starts with a single "Default" profile. It cannot be deleted until a second profile exists.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Locking — keep the preview pinned to a specific shader

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
The FPS display in the preview toolbar shows the live frame rate.

Click it to open the FPS menu:

  • Frame rate limit: Unlimited, 60 fps, or 30 fps
  • Performance: Toggle the performance panel

docs.title: Performance Panel
docs.text: The performance panel shows a real-time graph of your shader's rendering performance.

docs.title: Reading the Graph
docs.text:
The graph plots frame time (in milliseconds) on the Y-axis over recent history on the X-axis.

Reference lines:

Line Value Meaning Green 16.6ms 60 fps Red 33.3ms 30 fps Yellow Auto-detected Your screen refresh rate

A dashed line shows the average of the visible time window.

Switch between ms and fps views with the toggle buttons.

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text:
Below the graph, these statistics summarise the visible window and follow its zoom and pan:

Value Meaning p50 Typical frame time p95 The slowest 5% of frames — where a stutter appears first worst The slowest single frame late Number of frames that overran the window's own frame time by a whole refresh, holding the previous image on screen gpu How long the GPU took to finish a frame — see the note below on comparing shader languages

An average frame rate can look healthy while frames arrive unevenly, and uneven delivery is what the eye reads as stuttering. When the preview looks jumpy but the FPS display seems fine, check late and worst rather than the frame rate — a couple of late frames per second is enough to see, while barely moving the average.

Compare gpu with p50 before and after a change while using the same shader language. Measurements differ between GLSL and Slang/WGSL, so avoid direct comparisons between them. A much higher gpu value can mean the GPU is falling behind, even if the FPS display looks healthy.

Late measures uneven frame delivery at the shader's current rate. A shader running steadily at 30 fps has no late frames; occasional delays increase the count.

docs.title: Logging to the Console
docs.text: Use the toolbar's output button to log a performance summary to the developer console once per second. Copy the results to compare runs.

docs.title: Zoom and Pan
docs.text: Action Effect Drag Pan through history Ctrl + scroll Zoom Y-axis (1×–32×) Click zoom button Cycle Y-axis zoom Scroll Change the time window width Center button Re-center the visible area on the average

docs.title: Time Window
docs.text: A single button cycles through sample counts, showing more or less history. The default view is 180 frames (≈3 seconds at 60 fps).

docs.title: Downsample
docs.text: When viewing a long stretch of history, the downsample control averages frames together so the graph draws fewer points (1:1, 1:2, 1:4, 1:8). Higher values keep the graph responsive when zoomed out.

docs.title: Pause
docs.text: Click Pause to freeze the graph. Useful for inspecting a specific spike. Click again to resume. The graph also auto-pauses while you drag to pan.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• A spike above the 16.6ms line means a frame was rendered slower than 60 fps
  • Consistent high values suggest the shader is GPU-bound; try lowering the resolution scale
  • Zoom in vertically (Ctrl+scroll up) to magnify small variations
  • Pan left to examine earlier history

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Debug Mode — inspect and analyse your shader while it runs

docs.title: Recording
docs.text: Shader Studio can capture your shader output as a screenshot, video, or animated GIF.

docs.title: Opening the Recording Panel
docs.text: Click the Record button in the toolbar, or open Menu → Export.

docs.title: Screenshot
docs.text:
Capture a single frame as a PNG or JPEG. Live captures the pixels currently shown in the preview without changing shader time or resolution. Render creates a separate capture at a selected time and resolution.

Option Description Format PNG or JPEG Mode Live preview pixels, or a separate Render capture Capture frame at Shader time for Render mode: 0 or a time you enter. Preceding frames are rendered first. Resolution Current, 720p, 1080p, 4K, or custom dimensions in Render mode

Click Capture screenshot to save. Render mode simulates every preceding frame before the requested frame, so feedback buffers and iFrame match a continuous run rather than jumping directly to the selected time.

docs.title: Video
docs.text:
Record shader output as an MP4 (H.264) or WebM file. Live records the existing preview until you choose Stop & save; it does not restart the shader. Render produces a deterministic clip at a chosen time, duration, and resolution.

Option Description Format MP4 or WebM Mode Live preview recording, or a separate Render recording Start recording at Shader time for Render mode: 0 or a time you enter. Preceding frames are rendered first. Duration Render presets: 2π (≈6.3s), 5s, 10s, 30s, 60s, or custom FPS Screen, 24, 30, 60, or custom. In Render mode, Screen rounds to 24, 30, 60 or 120 fps Resolution Current, 720p, 1080p, 4K, or custom in Render mode

Available formats depend on your browser or VS Code's recording support. Unavailable formats are disabled. If a saved format is no longer available, the panel chooses a supported one and explains the change.

MP4 requires even pixel dimensions. If you choose an odd width or height, it is rounded up and the panel shows the saved size. Video quality adjusts automatically to preserve detail, so complex or fast-moving shaders can produce larger files.

Video stores colour at half resolution (4:2:0), so single-pixel coloured detail softens in any video file; use a PNG screenshot when exact colour per pixel matters. Render mode shows separate preparation, rendering, encoding, and saving phases. Click Cancel to abort a Render recording. During a Live recording, choose Discard or Stop & save. A Live recording keeps a fixed output size: if the preview is resized while recording, the preview is scaled until recording ends and then takes the new size. Editing the shader keeps recording. Opening a different shader stops the recording and saves what was recorded up to that point.

docs.title: GIF
docs.text:
Record an animated GIF.

Option Description Start recording at Shader time: 0 or a time you enter. Preceding frames are rendered first. Duration Presets or custom FPS 10, 15, 24, 30, or custom Loop Infinite or play once Quality 1–100 (higher = better quality, larger file)

An estimated file size is shown before recording. Captures that would require an unsafe amount of raw frame memory are rejected with guidance to reduce the duration, FPS, or resolution. Click Record to start.

Tips: - For shaders you usually want Quality 100 to preserve fine detail, but try reducing it if the file is too large - Lower FPS and resolution also produce smaller GIF files

docs.title: Capture state and settings
docs.text:
Render captures use the shader, pass settings, and current custom-uniform values from the moment capture begins. Later editor or script updates do not change a capture already in progress.

Each output remembers its own settings across reloads. Encoding, browser capability, memory, and save failures are shown in the Recording panel. Wait for saving to finish before closing the preview.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Live video is silent. It records the canvas only; shader audio inputs are not mixed into the file.
  • Render doesn't replay live input. Custom and script uniforms are a snapshot taken when the export starts and stay constant for the whole export. iMouse stays at its idle value, keyboard input is idle, and audio or video inputs play on the wall clock rather than the export timeline. The panel names the inputs your shader uses when this applies. Use Live to capture interaction.
  • Render preparation cost. A Render start time is reached by rendering every preceding frame from time 0 (at 60 fps for screenshots, at the export frame rate for video and GIF). Start times are limited to 3600 s.
  • Live recording smoothness depends on how fast the shader renders; a shader that stutters in the preview records the same stutter.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Open in Browser — preview your shader in a web browser

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text: The Resolution button in the preview toolbar shows the current canvas size. Click it to change how large the shader renders.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: Resolution changes through a simple toggle: Sync with Config.

docs.title: Sync with Config — On (Default)
docs.text:
When the checkbox is ticked, every change you make is saved to the shader's config file (.sha.json). The next time you open this shader, it will use the same resolution.

Use this when you want a specific resolution to stick with the shader — for example, forcing a 720p output for a particular effect.

docs.title: Sync with Config — Off
docs.text:
When the checkbox is unticked, your changes are session-only — they are not saved to the config file. The session override stays active for all shaders until you close Shader Studio or turn sync back on.

Use this when you want to temporarily test a different size — for example, dropping to half resolution to see if performance improves — without changing the saved config.

docs.title: Resolution Options
docs.text:
• Scale presets — Quick multipliers: 0.25x, 0.5x, 1x, 2x, 4x. Scale is applied on top of everything else.
  • Custom resolution — Type an exact width and height in pixels. When set, this overrides scale and aspect ratio.
  • Aspect ratio — 16:9, 4:3, 1:1 (square), Fill (use all available space), or Screen (match your screen).
  • Black background — Fill the area around the shader with black instead of the editor background.
  • Zoom — Magnify the preview visually without changing the actual render size (0.1x to 3.0x).

Tip

Scale still applies when custom resolution is set. For example, a custom size of 320 × 180 at 2x renders at 640 × 360.

docs.title: Setting Resolution in the Config Panel
docs.text:
You can also set the resolution from the Config panel. Open it from the toolbar, go to the Image tab, and set the resolution there. This is the same as using the toolbar with Sync with Config enabled.

See Configure Buffers and Inputs for the full guide on setting up passes, channels, and resolution through the config panel.

docs.title: Buffer Resolution
docs.text:
Buffer passes have their own resolution settings, but these can only be edited from the Config panel, not the resolution toolbar.

See Configure Buffers and Inputs for how to set buffer resolution.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Panel Layout — rearrange and dock panels

docs.title: Shader Explorer
docs.text: Shader Explorer lets you browse, search, and preview all shader files in your workspace.

docs.title: Opening
docs.text:
The Shader Explorer is available in two forms — the sidebar for persistent browsing, and the full panel for focused exploration.

  • Sidebar — click the Shader Studio icon in the VS Code activity bar. The explorer appears as a sidebar view you can keep open alongside your editor.
  • Full panel — open the toolbar menu and choose Shader Explorer, or run Shader Studio: Open Shader Explorer from the command palette.

Each view remembers its own search, sorting, page, and card-size choices.

docs.title: Browsing and Navigation
docs.text:
Each shader in your workspace appears as a card showing a live-rendered thumbnail preview, the shader filename, and its last-modified date.

  • Click a card to open the shader file in the editor and refresh its thumbnail preview.
  • Right-click a card to open a context menu with options to open the shader, open its config, or delete it.
  • Open file when selecting a shader — when enabled, clicking a card opens the shader file in the editor. Turn this off to change the preview without opening its file. This control is hidden while Only keep active shader files open manages the editor tabs.

docs.title: Keep Files with Their Preview
docs.text:
Open Explorer settings (the gear button), find Files, and enable Only keep active shader files open. It is on by default in standalone and off by default in VS Code. VS Code also exposes it as shader-studio.explorer.keepActiveShaderFiles in Settings.

The active preview opens its main shader, linked buffer, Common and vertex sources. The .sha.json config is not opened automatically. Switching to another shader opens that shader's files and closes shader tabs outside the active previews, including shader files you opened separately. Closing a tab does not delete its file. Other tabs, such as notes or a README, stay open.

In VS Code, each preview maintains its own editor group. With two previews, switching one replaces its file set while the other preview's files stay open. A locked preview keeps its own files until its displayed shader changes or the preview closes. Standalone currently provides one preview pane.

If an old file has unsaved changes, closing it asks first. VS Code uses its usual save dialog; Cancel keeps that file open. Standalone normally saves automatically, but pending or failed saves prompt you to save and close; cancelling or a failed save keeps the file open. Saved files close without a prompt. Cancelling does not undo the preview switch.

Turning the setting off leaves the current tabs open and stops managing them. The feature uses each preview's known source files; it does not search other shaders' configs to guess ownership.

docs.title: Search and Sort
docs.text:
• Search — type in the search bar to filter shaders by name, path, or shader source text (case-insensitive). Name matches are shown before path and source-text matches. Multiple terms are combined, quoted phrases match exactly, and terms prefixed with - are excluded, e.g. ray sphere -buffer or "ray march".
  • Sort by — dropdown with options:
    • Name — alphabetical A–Z
    • Updated — most recently modified first
    • Created — newest first
  • Sort order — toggle button to switch ascending/descending

docs.title: Display Options
docs.text:
Click the gear button to open Explorer settings over the shader list. Settings are grouped into Display, Filters, and Files and save immediately. Close with the × button, Escape, or a click outside. Reset to defaults restores all Display, Filters and Files options, including the host-specific default for active shader files.

  • Card size — slider (100–1000px width) to control how large shader cards appear. Only available in grid layout mode.
  • Layout — toggle between Grid (cards in a responsive grid) and List (cards in a single-column list with larger thumbnails).
  • Per page — dropdown to show 10, 20, 30, 50, or 100 shaders per page.
  • Hide buffer files and Hide vertex files — hide matching buffer and vertex filenames from the explorer.
  • Hide failed previews — checkbox to hide shaders that failed to compile or render.
  • Open file when selecting a shader — controls whether clicking a card opens its file when automatic file management is off.
  • Only keep active shader files open — opens and retires file sets with the active previews, as described above.

docs.title: Refresh
docs.text:
Shader Explorer updates by itself when shader or .sha.json files are added, changed, or deleted, and redraws the affected thumbnails.

Click the refresh button in the toolbar to re-scan the workspace for shaders and regenerate all thumbnails.

Clicking an individual shader card also refreshes that shader's thumbnail — useful after editing a shader to update its preview in the explorer.

docs.title: File Management
docs.text:
• New shader — click the + button in the toolbar to create a new shader file from a template.
  • Delete shader — right-click a card and choose Delete to move the shader file to the trash. If the shader has dependent buffer pass files, a confirmation dialog warns you before deleting.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Code Snippets — insert bundled shader code through native VS Code completion

docs.title: Slang Support
docs.text:
Slang shaders (.slang) run on WebGPU in the VS Code extension and standalone browser. Built-in fragment shaders define mainImage, vertex shaders use the vertex hook, and compute passes declare [shader("compute")] entry points. A WebGPU-capable host is required.

Slang supports multipass rendering, Common helpers, storage buffers, textures, cubemaps, audio/video, keyboard input, module imports, model geometry, and script uniforms. See Channels for channel metadata and sampling.

docs.title: Native entry points
docs.text:
Slang supports the same shared-file workflow and entry-point configuration as WGSL. Declare stages with [shader("vertex")], [shader("fragment")], and [shader("compute")], then choose them in the config panel. Native render outputs use SV_Position and SV_Target0 (or SV_TargetN for multiple render targets); compute uses [numthreads(x, y, z)]. Built-in uniforms, channel helpers, and configured storage remain available. Image and buffer passes can select different fragments from the same source. Vertex and fragment selection is independent, so native stages can be paired with mainVertex or mainImage adapters. Mesh camera matrices are available as iModelMatrix, iViewProjectionMatrix, and iNormalMatrix; multiply with mul(matrix, vector) to follow the viewer camera.

New compute configuration uses entryPoints.compute; the older entryPoint field still loads for compatibility. Choose Add function… under the relevant stage to append code to its selected source. File → Change… lets you reuse a config file, browse the workspace, or create a source file. Compute uses native functions directly; render stages offer Built-in hooks or Native entry points.

docs.title: Channels
docs.text: Every configured channel is a direct Slang global. For example, use albedo.Sample(uv), albedo.SampleLevel(uv, 0.0), and albedo.size for a channel named albedo. inputs.albedo was removed; migrate old shaders by removing inputs. from channel access. The .sha.json inputs field still defines the channel bindings. Shared sample2D and sampleCube functions and direct channel methods remain available. See Channels for sampling rules and reserved-name diagnostics.

docs.title: Editing
docs.text:
Completion, hover, signature help, definitions, references, highlights, and symbol rename are available. Hover shows types for locals, parameters, struct fields, vector components, channel methods, and storage buffers. Signature help follows nested and generic calls. See Language Servers for rename instructions and limitations.

The editor reports errors and marks unused locals and parameters. Entry parameters with an SV_ semantic are not marked as unused.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
Use inline rendering to preview a value and the Variable Inspector to capture supported locals, parameters, and return values. Common helpers and values read from storage are supported. float2x2 values capture as four components; larger matrices cannot be captured as a whole. Select a column or scalar component instead. Vertex-stage debugging is unavailable.

Compute inline previews and variable capture inspect one invocation at a time without updating the pass's output texture. Read-only storage access is supported, but workgroup memory, barriers, subgroup operations, atomics on workgroup memory, and configured storage writes are not supported during compute debugging. These restrictions apply to compute debugging, not normal compute rendering. Fragment-stage subgroup previews remain available.

Compute debugging cannot reproduce threads working together in a workgroup. Avoid relying on it to inspect side effects hidden in imported code or complex macros.

See Language Support to compare GLSL, Slang, and WGSL.

For WebGPU mesh geometry, Use viewer camera defaults on. Turn it off to use mesh or mainVertex positions directly in clip space, without the viewer rotation, view, or perspective transform. Native vertex stages that read iModelMatrix, iViewProjectionMatrix, and iNormalMatrix receive identity matrices when it is off; stages with their own projection continue to control their output. The per-pass setting saves as useViewerCamera: false on Image or Buffer. Fullscreen vertex stages already use clip space. GLSL mesh passes also respect this setting.

Opening a different shader resets the 3D viewer camera’s orbit, pan, and zoom. Editing or recompiling the current shader preserves the view.

Change the global camera default in VS Code Settings (Shader Studio › WebGPU: Use Viewer Camera) or standalone’s top-level Settings → Use viewer camera. Image and buffer passes can override it with Use viewer camera; Use default clears that pass override. Pass choices are saved as passes.<name>.useViewerCamera. The global preference is stored as shader-studio.webgpu.useViewerCamera in VS Code user settings and in browser storage in standalone, and is never copied into .sha.json files. Existing shader-wide webgpu.useViewerCamera settings in JSON remain supported between the pass and global defaults. Defaults remain enabled for older projects.

docs.title: GPU Storage
docs.text: Storage buffers keep data, such as particle positions or simulation values, between passes and frames. They are available to Slang and WGSL shaders on devices with WebGPU support. A compute pass can update a buffer, then a vertex or fragment pass can read those values to draw the result. Your shader accesses the buffer by its configured name.

docs.title: Workspace layout
docs.text:
Open the config panel and select a card labeled Storage buffer, such as particles. Each storage buffer has its own card alongside the shader passes; selecting it opens its Settings and Inspect tabs directly. Use + New → Storage buffer to create a declaration. This is also available when the shader has no storage yet.

In Settings, edit the name, element count, layout and initialization. Changes stay in the current editor until you click Apply changes, either above or below the settings. Both buttons use the same validation and save action. The header button appears only while changes are pending. Cancel restores the saved settings. Apply or cancel before selecting another card or switching tabs; leaving the editor discards its pending changes. Renaming a buffer updates its card; deleting it removes the card.

docs.title: Element layout
docs.text:
Choose a scalar or vector type, a struct defined in shader source, or define numeric struct fields in the config. Config-defined fields generate the corresponding Slang or WGSL struct automatically. The settings show the element stride, allocation size and generated declaration.

Use distinct field names and match your binary data to the displayed layout. GPU alignment matters: an array of vec3<f32> has a 16-byte stride even though each vector holds 12 bytes of values. Struct fields can also contain padding. Fields are not tightly packed automatically.

Buffers are available to every pass. Shader code determines which ones it accesses. The pass list describes this access model; it does not connect or disconnect buffers. Compute passes can read and write; vertex and fragment passes have read-only access.

docs.title: Initial data and reset
docs.text:
Start with chooses zeros or Binary files. Click Select to pick each file and + Add file for another. Set each destination Byte offset from the start of the buffer, in decimal or hexadecimal (for example 0x00200000). Use the arrows to change the load order, then apply the changes.

The config stores an ordered initialDataFiles list of { path, byteOffset } entries. Paths resolve like texture paths: relative to the shader, @/ for workspace-relative, or absolute. An omitted offset means zero. The buffer starts at zero, then each file's complete raw bytes are copied in list order. Later files overwrite any overlapping bytes. There is no fixed file size cap, but each offset plus file length must fit in the allocated buffer. A missing or oversized file fails the compile and leaves installed storage alone. Keep the data files alongside your shader.

Initial data is not converted: the file's raw bytes are copied as-is. Supply bytes matching the shader's numeric representation (little-endian on every WebGPU device), field offsets and array stride. For example, two float4 elements need eight 32-bit floats (32 bytes).

Between frames defaults to keeping previous values. Clear every frame zeros the buffer before each normal simulation frame; it does not reload the binary initial data each frame. Paused redraws do not perform that clear.

Reset when the shader restarts is enabled by default. Turning it off preserves an existing compatible buffer during a restart. Opening a different shader or changing the buffer's layout, size, initial data file or that file's contents can allocate fresh storage. Compatible declarations preserve their contents across ordinary recompiles.

Reset data now reloads the selected buffer's files, clears the buffer and reapplies them in list order. A load failure preserves the current contents. Apply or cancel pending edits first. This resets the buffer data; it does not rerun compute passes.

Remove buffer deletes the declaration. Remove any compute dispatch targets referring to it first, and update shader code that still uses its name.

docs.title: Inspecting values
docs.text:
Inspect shows the buffer's current values without changing them. Scalars appear as an index/value list; vectors show each component in a separate column. For structs, select one numeric field at a time. The selected field is remembered for each buffer and shader.

Use Capture snapshot for a single read, or Start live for updates up to twice per second. Inspect pages of up to 16 elements using the first-element control and navigation buttons. Integer values can be shown in decimal or hexadecimal. Snapshot details include the frame and capture point when available.

The Capture point choices refer to GPU execution, not file edits:

Choice What it reads Latest values The selected buffer's contents when the read is requested; this also works while paused. Before a pass Contents just before that pass next executes. After a pass Contents just after that pass next executes.

Passes marked Run once, such as an initialization pass named Seed, are excluded from before/after choices: their next execution may already have happened. Read their resulting data with Latest values. For other pass capture points, resume the shader so the selected pass can run. A pass that does not execute produces a capture-point error rather than invented values.

Numeric scalar and vector fields from config-defined and source-defined structs can be inspected. Matrices, nested structs and array fields remain valid shader types but are not displayed as numeric fields. The inspector reports unsupported layouts explicitly. Field comparison and editing GPU values are not part of this layout.

See Compute Passes for shader examples and Config File Format for the JSON fields.

docs.title: WGSL Storage Types
docs.text: Use native WGSL types in the storage configuration, such as f32, vec3f, atomic<u32>, or a struct declared in your shader or Common code. Buffer sizes are calculated automatically, including padding, nested arrays and structs, and @align / @size attributes. Half-precision types require enable f16; and GPU support for shader-f16. For buffers of f16 scalars, use an even element count if your shader relies on arrayLength; an odd count includes an extra padding element.

docs.title: Time and Playback Controls
docs.text: Time controls let you scrub through shader animations, loop specific time ranges, and adjust playback speed.

docs.title: Opening
docs.text: Click the time display (e.g. 42.53s) in the toolbar to expand the time controls menu.

docs.title: Time Scrubbing
docs.text:
Drag the time slider to manually set the shader time. The shader updates in real time as you scrub.

When loop mode is enabled, the slider range matches the selected loop duration. When loop is off, the slider covers the full elapsed time.

docs.title: Loop Mode
docs.text: Click the loop button to enable looping. When active, shader time wraps around at the end of the selected duration.

docs.title: Duration Presets and Custom Ranges
docs.text:
Quick buttons to set the loop range:

Preset Duration Use Case 2π 6.28s Trigonometric cycles (sin(iTime), cos(iTime)) 10s 10s Short animations 30s 30s Medium animations 1m 60s Longer sequences 2m 120s Extended animations

Use the custom seconds input next to the presets for exact loop ranges, such as 2.2 seconds. Custom loop durations must be positive and only apply while loop mode is enabled.

docs.title: Playback Speed
docs.text: Adjust how fast time advances with the speed slider or preset buttons. The slider covers common speeds from 0.25x to 4.0x in 0.25 increments.

docs.title: Speed Presets and Custom Speeds
docs.text:
Preset Use Case 0.25x Slow motion — inspect fast animations frame by frame 0.5x Half speed — see timing details 1x Normal speed 2x Double speed — quickly preview long animations 4x Fast forward

Use the custom speed input next to the presets for exact multipliers, including values outside the slider range. For example, 0.01 runs time very slowly, 0 freezes playback, 12.5 previews much faster than the 4x preset, and -1 runs time backward.

docs.title: Uniforms
docs.text: Uniforms are how a shader reads values that change per frame or per setup: time, resolution, mouse state, input channels, and your own custom parameters. Shader Studio declares the built-ins for you and can read custom ones from a Script pass.

docs.title: Built-in uniforms
docs.text:
These are always available — no declaration needed. Types differ slightly between GLSL, Slang, and WGSL:

Uniform GLSL Slang WGSL Meaning iResolution vec3 float3 vec3f Canvas size in xy, aspect ratio in z iTime float float f32 Elapsed time in seconds iTimeDelta float float f32 Time since the previous frame iFrameRate float float f32 Current frames per second iMouse vec4 float4 vec4f As on Shadertoy: xy = pointer position while a button is held, zw = click position; z > 0 while held, w > 0 only on the click frame iPointer struct struct struct Hover, individual mouse buttons, modifiers and scrolling; see below iFrame int int i32 Frame counter starting at zero iDate vec4 float4 vec4f Year, month, day, seconds since midnight iChannelTime float[1024] — — Playback time per input channel iChannelResolution vec3[1024] — — Resolution per input channel iSampleRate float float f32 Audio sample rate in hertz iCameraPos vec3 float3 vec3f Camera position in world space iCameraDir vec3 float3 vec3f Normalised camera look direction iVertexCount int uint u32 Vertices drawn by the pass: the vertices geometry's vertexCount (default 3), 3 for fullscreen, or the mesh vertex count iInstanceCount int uint u32 Copies of the geometry the pass draws: the geometry's instanceCount (default 1), or 1 for fullscreen iViewMatrix mat4 float4x4 mat4x4f The orbit camera's view matrix (world to view space) iProjectionMatrix mat4 float4x4 mat4x4f The orbit camera's perspective projection at the pass's aspect ratio iViewProjection mat4 float4x4 mat4x4f iProjectionMatrix * iViewMatrix: world space to clip space. See Camera matrices iInstanceIndex int uint u32 Which copy is being drawn, from 0 to iInstanceCount - 1; fragments get the value of the copy that drew them. See Instancing iChannel0–iChannel3 sampler2D (or cube/3D) ShaderStudioChannel2D / …Cube / …3D Metadata object; use iChannel0Texture and iChannel0Sampler to sample Input channel textures in configured slot order iCh0–iCh3 channel metadata struct — — Input channel with sampler, size, playback time, and loaded state <name> named channel object ShaderStudioChannel2D / …Cube / …3D Metadata object; use <name>Texture and <name>Sampler to sample Input channel configured with that name iDispatch — int i32 Compute only: zero-based dispatch index iWorldPosition vec3 float3 vec3f Fragment only: world-space position of the fragment; zero for fullscreen geometry iNormal vec3 float3 vec3f Fragment only: world-space interpolated normal; zero for fullscreen geometry iCameraPosition vec3 float3 vec3f Fragment only: world-space camera position for mesh fragments; zero for fullscreen geometry iVertexUv vec2 float2 vec2f Fragment only: perspective-correct interpolated uv written by mainVertex, for every geometry and space iFrontFacing bool bool bool Fragment only: whether the current primitive is front-facing; always true for fullscreen geometry

iVertexUv and iFrontFacing are available for every geometry and space. iWorldPosition, iNormal, and iCameraPosition carry values only when the pass renders 3D geometry — see Vertex Shaders.

Slang has no iChN, iChannelTime, or iChannelResolution symbols. Each configured channel is a direct global named by its exact configuration key — iChannel0 stays iChannel0, and a channel named noise is noise — with metadata such as noise.size, noise.time, and noise.loaded. The former inputs.<name> syntax was removed; only the .sha.json configuration still uses its inputs field.

WGSL also has no iChN, iChannelTime, or iChannelResolution symbols. Its direct channel global provides metadata such as noise.size, noise.time, and noise.loaded; native handles are separate (noiseTexture and noiseSampler). Use sample2D(noiseTexture, noiseSampler, uv) or the legacy noiseSample(uv) helper. See Channels for the complete channel API and stage-specific sampling rules.

docs.title: Custom uniforms
docs.text:
Add a Script pass in the config panel to compute custom uniform values each frame from TypeScript or JavaScript:

// shader.uniforms.ts
export function uniforms(ctx: { time: number }) {
  return {
    uSpeed: 1.5,
    uOffset: [0.1, 0.2],
  };
}

Types are inferred from the return value on the first call. Supported types: float, vec2, vec3, vec4, bool — in Slang they arrive as float, float2, float3, float4, and bool; in WGSL, as f32, vec2f, vec3f, vec4f, and bool. The values are available automatically — use uSpeed and uOffset in your shader with no declaration. See The Script Pass for exporting, polling, and Node.js APIs.
